records.storyText:
Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

It can talk(kinda)

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

records.title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape
records.author: rvanderlinden
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Ruud, co-founder of Lont. We turn company emails into personalized videos.

Video captions cost us manual work twice: fixing misheard words, then fixing layout, like lines ending on “the”.

Overtone uses multiple models to listen to the audio: gpt-transcribe, Azure STT, and Elevenlabs Scribe. When they return conflicting results, Overtone sends small clips to the models again, and then lets an LLM decide what was actually said.

The LLM is like a human doing a sanity check on the transcription model. Humans would easily recognize a word to be different based on context. The LLM basically does the same, using an optional context prompt + its world knowledge. Because of this the Word Error Rate (WER) on many test files is lower when using Overtone, compared to just using a model without it.

Sure, the cost is higher because we use up to 3 different STT models + an LLM, but it still removes mistakes, reducing the time needed to fix captions to a minimum, and reducing the chance you'll miss something. For us it's worth it. For ultra high volume use cases it may not be.

The rules-based cutter nicely cuts the transcript into captions that look good, depending on screen size: 16:9 is different from 9:16, and the Overtone Format we created supports any type really. Pauses become breaks, captions are grouped per speaker, and names/numbers are never spread out over multiple captions.

How to add these captions to your videos? A videojs plugin can do this automatically, so you don't burn in your captions. The plugin lets you cycle between styled captions, plain captions, and off. You can burn them into an MP4 file with overtone burn.

Quickly try it out just the cutter? Try:

  npx overtone-captions recut yoursub.srt
Transcribing audio with API keys works too. Use --dry-run to show a cost estimate before you send.

We open-sourced this first version (MIT) because we believe many people can benefit from this, especially if your captions just need to be good. There's plenty of room to improve though, so we've made it easy to help contribute to add style packs, languages, and providers/models.

You can find a demo at: https://overtone.lont.ai/

Find the code and benchmarks here: https://github.com/lonthq/overtone-captions

records.title: Show HN: Lasm – Write formally verified webapps in Lean for Node/serverless/edge
records.author: lastmjs
records.storyText:
Lasm has been my dream for a good part of 2026. I firmly believe that formal verification is the next evolution of software engineering and programming languages. This next wave will largely be enabled by the incredibly intelligent LLMs that understand formal verification and its programming languages.

Lean is one of the most popular languages that allow for formal verification, and to me is incredibly powerful because it is a general purpose programming language with formal verification built directly into it.

You can build general purpose software in Lean, and formally verify it in Lean. Amazing.

Lasm brings Lean to the browser, Node, serverless, and edge environments (and more). The idea is that you can now write web apps, frontend to backend, in Lean and formally verify these apps.

Imagine an Express server or Hono server, running on Cloudflare Workers, with formal verification of its specification.

I'm an agentic engineer with an emphasis in software engineering, and Lasm was built mostly by Claude Opus 5.5 with my high-level direction.

records.title: Show HN: Sketch Stadium – watch your agent play Pictionary
records.author: ericlevine
records.storyText:
tl;dr: Agents can play Pictionary. You can connect your own agent, or just watch a game in progress here: https://sketch.wakeshift.ai/games/q5ucru

Hi folks! I initially built this as a proof-of-concept for sending push notifications to AI agents. Watching the agents play Pictionary together has been compelling, so I thought I'd ship it as a standalone demonstration.

In Sketch Stadium, your agent subscribes to game events. Agents take turns either drawing or guessing. Easy clues are 1 point, medium are 2, and hard are 3. It's entertaining to watch and some of the drawings are impressive (and others are mind-bogglingly bad). This is the real opportunity for the model labs who have been pelican-maxxing to shine.

The first version gave agents the ability to draw lines 10 at a time so that it would be a little bit more like real Pictionary. However, it turns out agents are _really_ bad at drawing that way. So instead I let them use a subset of SVG to draw and that's worked much better, even for the lower-cost models.

You don't need to create an account to connect your agent, just add the MCP and authorize. But if you don't want to do that, just watch the game linked above.

As a bit more background, agents often start processes that take an indeterminate amount of time to complete (e.g. CI, waiting for approval in a separate system, sending an email and waiting for a reply). If an agent needs that process to complete before it can proceed, it can:

* poll,

* ask the user to tell it when it's done,

* use a bespoke built-in integration, or

* use a proprietary capability (e.g. Claude Code monitors)

Today, there's no easy, consistent way to wake up agents through a webhook or push notification. I dealt with this firsthand with Clawvisor (authorization for agents) where I needed agents to recognize when the operator had clicked an out-of-band approve button. The best-supported way to achieve that at the time was long-polling.

This project is basically a tech demo for Wakeshift, which is a cross-harness, simple SDK for providing push notifications for agents. It attaches to your MCP to allow consumers of your MCP to subscribe to real-time events, and uses whatever available hacks per harness to wake an agent when dormant. For most harnesses, Wakeshift requires a hook to be installed for the best experience. It will upgrade automatically as harnesses start adopting MCP events.

I'd love any feedback or ideas for other products or games that you'd want to see built on this capability. Or MCP servers that you use today that you think would benefit from push notifications.

records.title: Show HN: Artificer by Nua: Frontier robotics task evaluation in 4B parameters
records.author: SunnyWan
records.storyText:
We’re happy to introduce Artificer, our first robotics decision model for evaluating robot task progress and success. The problem Robot systems need feedback during training, evaluation, and deployment. An arm might grasp the right object, but place it in the wrong bin. A robot might’ve only completed part of its task before it stopped. Assessing these outcomes from video often requires manual review or brittle, handcrafted objectives. Though frontier models do well in evaluation, they are expensive and slow. Artificer is a 4B parameter model that estimates task completion and progress, at the frontier level, from a task description and video. During deployment, these estimates provide feedback to a robot controller to help decide whether to continue an attempt, retry, or move to the next task.

Know a robotics team working on task evaluation or success detection? We'd appreciate an introduction! For the robotics founders: we’d love to test Artificer on your task videos! Would love to chat more in the comments or over email! sunny@trynua.dev

records.title: Show HN: Fast agentic video editing in the browser (Tella)
records.author: 9ranty
records.storyText:
Hi HN, today we're launching the biggest update to Tella ever (https://tella.com/).

Tella is all-in-one video creation. You can record, edit and publish with one tool. Today we're shipping:

1. Tella Agent: An in-app video editing agent 2. Tella Motion: Rich motion graphics support 3. Auto Capture: Agentic screen recording

Our in-app agent uses the same tools as our MCP. All year we've been exposing more of our editor to the MCP. So when we started working on the in-app agent a few weeks ago, agents could already do a lot. Since then, we've worked hard to add as much capability as possible to the MCP. So whether you're editing on tella.com or from Claude Code you get the same capabilities.

With the agent you can do all obvious agentic video editing stuff, like cut silences, fillers and mistakes. You can also do batch actions that would normally take a long time by hand. For example, if your tutorial video has a lot of zoom effects, you can ask the agent to adjust the scale for certain zooms: "for all zooms applied to when I'm showing Google Chrome, reduce them to 150%".

But you can push it further with ambitious long-form edits and editing multiple videos at the same time.

LLMs have proven to be very good at motion graphics. Remotion and Hyperframes launched earlier this year with React and HTML-based motion graphics respectively. We took a different approach and built our own motion graphics primitives on top of Skia and WebGPU. This means we're not limited by the DOM and can support things like liquid glass, motion blur, and text that moves along a path. We can also render a lot faster than DOM-based approaches because we can bypass Chrome and run everything directly on a GPU.

But motion graphics are much more about how they look and feel rather than how they work. I've asked our agent to create motion graphics for animated UI, collage stop motion scenes, realistic paint splatters and photographic filters - the quality of the output continues to surprise me.

Tella began life as a screen recording tool and today's update brings our origins into the AI era. Auto Capture is our new agentic screen recording tool. You can give it a website and a goal and it will remotely record itself using Chrome, completing your task.

There are lots of other agentic browser tools with screen recording support, but we couldn't find any that were fit for "marketing grade" videos, i.e. recordings done in 4K at 60fps. So we built our own.

For this to be practical (i.e. make demos of your own product) it needs to handle auth, so Auto Capture has a 1Password integration to handle signing into your sites and dealing with MFA.

We also capture synthetic cursor data and keyboard shortcuts so that the Tella editor can add an animated cursor, animated keyboard shortcuts, and apply zoom effects.

You can try all of this in your browser or connect to our MCP.

Let me know what you think.

Announcement + video here: https://x.com/9ranty/status/2115797158519550360

records.title: Show HN: KernelCash – Privacy First Budgeting
records.author: LoftyHobbitMan
records.storyText:
Hi everyone! I typically do not put my projects out for others to see, so this is new to me, but I have created a privacy first budgeting app called KernelCash Budgets ( https://kernelcash.com ), and wanted to share it here in the event someone was interested in a product like this. This app has really helped my wife and I, as well as some family, friends, and colleagues, so I wanted to put this out to see if it could help anyone else.

I created this app as a replacement to some of the other budgeting apps out there. Some of KernelCash's core features include:

- Envelope and zero style budgeting - Expense, income, and savings goal tracking - Full analytics for income, expenses, and savings - Bank connection / sync free. We use transaction file imports (OFX / QFX) or manual entry to keep things private. You can freely share or not share what you choose. - Multi-collaborator workspaces. These are great for sharing your budget with a spouse, roommates, and have even been used by some parents to teach their kids how to budget. Each workspace is an independent sandbox for you to choose how you work with it. - Customizable budgets that are not month-locked. You control the time span of each budget you have. - There is only one pricing tier so you will always get every feature.

I initially created this app only for my wife and I and ran it on a Raspberry Pi. I made it well over a year ago as a replacement for some of the other budgeting apps that I had been using and trying out. I have used many of the budgeting apps that are out there, and a lot of them were either cumbersome to get my data into, or wanted all of my financial data along with bank account connections. Needless to say, I was not really happy with any of these, and so that's why I chose to build KernelCash.

KernelCash started as a small tool for my wife and I that I created as a hobby project so that I learn new skills for my day job, and to scratch some of the coding and architectural itches I don't get at work (I'm a software engineer). I never intended to release this to the public, but over time KernelCash came up while in conversations with friends, family, and colleagues. Many of them were really interested in it and wanted to use it since they apparently had some of the same privacy concerns as I did. Since they were wanting access to the app, I decided to move it out of my homelab and into a real multi-tenant application with all of the customer service, landing pages, and other gismos that are expected with a production app. As expected, that was more work than the core app logic.

We are priced lower than essentially all of the alternatives at $9.99/month or $87.50 for the annual subscription.

If I had the financial means to, I would give this away for free. I can't justify maintaining this project and work full-time and have a family, so I have priced the product as low as I can based on server / infra + general admin and development costs of running this product.

We offer a one month free trial and welcome anyone who is curious to try out the product and give any feedback you may have.

Feel free to ask any questions, I would love to answer them!

You can find KernelCash at https://kernelcash.com

Edit: Fixed URL.

records.title: Show HN: We mapped data center regulations across 50 states and 1,462 localities
records.author: pensono
records.storyText:
Hi HN! My company Regbase tracks regulatory developments around the world for compliance teams at major corporations. Ahead of the midterm elections we decided to do an in-depth survey of all state and local regulations around data centers.

We built an interactive map showing the data center policies across the United States. It covers all 50 states and 1,462 localities across legislation, regulations and executive orders. We collected and analyzed the data using our platform. Every result has a link to the official source so you can read the policy for yourself.

Here's some interesting things we learned:

- Moratoriums (temporary bans) are the most common instrument. We counted 1,010 in total with an average duration of 10 months.

- Starting around October 2025, most policies switched from tax incentives to bans and restrictions. This correlates with increased energy prices and worsening public sentiment towards AI.

- When construction is allowed, it's very common for protections to be put in place particularly around electricity and less for water. Many of the bans are actually refusals to issue these licenses.

We would love your feedback! In particular please let us know if there is any other data that would be useful or interesting to see.

records.title: Show HN: Pretty Git Tree – Your Git history as generative art
records.author: hda-hda
records.storyText:
I've spent months building something complex and (so far) invisible. I know that the number of commits, branches, merges etc. aren't proof of progress, but what I needed was a way to represent the amount of effort I'd put in that wasn't "proximity to burnout".

Pretty-git-tree takes in your git history (just the commit structure, and it stays local to your browser) and gives you a visually interesting representation of it. For my own projects I use the "qubits" style which winds a quantum circuit around a space-filling curve. I've included snapshots of some famous git repositories as well.

I didn't want to just use the standard git tree, because I felt that there were so many different ways of exploring the data - plus I wanted it to look good at the top of a weekly standup report. I've included the four styles I expect people to use, plus another 15 or so styles in the repo where I wanted to try things out (like rendering the branches as tower-blocks in a city, or kintsugi fractures). The repo itself is MIT licensed, and suggestions are welcome.

records.title: Show HN: Beolis – Manage your coding AI agents
records.author: fabioz
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm Fabio, the creator of Beolis.

I've built Beolis (https://beolis.com) to better handle coding on agentic scenarios.

It can be used to manage coding with agents in parallel / in the background either in your local machine (using your current repository or git worktrees) or remotely (where it creates a git worktree remotely and works with the agent there).

Although it uses agents you don't need to "chat" with the agent at each step as you usually do when dealing with agents (although you still can), but rather create workflows where you can code the default steps you want. This means that instead of saying 'run the tests' to an agent the idea is that you (or the agent) create code that will actually run the tests and then if it fails it goes to a cheap agent to summarize the failures and then onto a smarter agent to actually do the fixes and work on the problems found -- I find my tokens last much longer given that approach ;)

I've been using Beolis to build itself (started back in February) and I believe it's now stable for day-to-day use.

For local use it's completely free, otherwise, you can get more collaboration features and remote workers.

I'd love to hear feedback.

I've built this completely solo over the last month. I posted here once a few weeks ago at a very early stage, but since it has greatly matured and I feel is legitimate for a repost.

We all know "We stand on the shoulders of giants", but who's shoulders exactly? This application is meant to help anyone answer this for themselves, their advisor, or just a scholar they are curious about - anywhere in the world.

Current Challenges I'm facing are largely surrounding PDF extractions which I aim to complete as many templates as possible to reduce the token costs incurred running the worst of them through an LLM for ingestion.

records.title: Show HN: Apgar – Catch agent regressions without an LLM judge
records.author: jtkm6
records.storyText:
Hey HN, We build financial AI agents, and Apgar is the tool we wrote to see whether a harness change made an agent better or worse in production. Our offline evals can't cover every kind of question or session real users bring, and the LLM judge we run in Langfuse is too expensive to use on more than a small slice of traffic, so some failures get through.

Apgar is a small release health checker that sits on top of our Langfuse data. It picks up the release from the production traces, and for the first hours of each new release it compares the agent's behavior with the previous release on things like tool calls per turn, retries of the same failing call, loops, output length and cost per turn (11 metrics right now). The release page shows what moved in both directions. When something gets worse, we get a Slack message (and a webhook) saying which metric moved and where the change is concentrated, for example only on Telegram or only in long sessions. We've been running it for a while and decided to open-source it: https://github.com/oimo-ai/apgar

It's not meant to be another monitoring tool. We still use Langfuse for that. Apgar only tries to answer "is this release worse than the last one?" It works with Langfuse or with anything that sends OpenTelemetry. There's no LLM judge in it, so it's cheap enough to run on all traffic. The downside is that it can't tell that an answer is wrong if everything else about the turn looks the same. That's still what our evals are for.

It runs on Docker Compose (or Helm) with ClickHouse, and it's Apache-2.0. The Agents page can load demo data if you want to try it without connecting anything.

Curious how others deal with this. When you change your harness or prompts, how do you find out whether the agent actually got better or worse?

records.title: Show HN: Keyward – a TUI to manage SSH keys and audit your –/.ssh security
records.author: weiqur
records.storyText:
Hi HN! Today I wanna show you a thing that solved my headache (and maybe will solve yours too). The only reason I created this tool is a mess around my SSH keys and configs. I am constantly working with a bunch of devices via SSH (such as Raspberry Pi's, VPS, handmade NAS, etc.) and I never knew whether permissions were right and there was no way to tell a strong key from a weak one. So, meet Keyward

Main features:

1. Lists every key with algorithm, size, fingerprint, comment, date of last modification and whether it has a passphrase

2. Runs a security audit for all of your keys, config and permissions in ~/.ssh and grades the result with A-F score. Also here you can find fix suggestions for every problem

3. Editor for ~/.ssh/config with byte-identical round-trip so all your comments are untouched

4. Convenient key generator for those who have difficulties using the "ssh-keygen" command

5. Backup of your keys, config and encrypted metadata so u can move all of your files quickly and safely and restore them on another machine

6. Headless CLI, e.g. keyward audit --json --fail-on=warning

7. Look through your known_hosts file to see address, key type and fingerprint and delete unnecessary records

Private keys are deliberately NOT encrypted by Keyward, they stay protected by their own passphrases.

No daemon, no network calls, no config to learn before starting, just a single static Go binary. The security-sensitive core's direct dependencies are only filippo.io/age and golang.org/x/crypto, releases are cosign-signed. Threat model is in SECURITY.md

Install:

   brew install gateway-of-last-resort/tap/keyward for macOS/Linux,
   yay -S keyward-bin for Arch Linux
   binary / go install for Windows
I would love feedback, especially on audit checks: what SSH misconfig should it catch that it doesn't?

records.title: Show HN: SpecDeck – Bring coding agent decisions back into the spec
records.author: specdeck
records.storyText:
Writing good specs is hard. You don’t know everything upfront and it’s impossible to write every little detail in the spec. Much of my job as a developer has been to treat specs as intent, and fill out the blanks in the code and use the code reviews as a way to question those decisions. But as coding agents have started to produce much more code, the decisions that actually affect the product are getting harder to find.

So I created SpecDeck. It helps everyone on the team write specs and hand them over to developers and their agents through MCP. During implementation, agents write the decisions that matter back as proposed spec changes and leave smaller implementation choices in the code. When the work is done, a person reviews and publish those changes into the spec.

The workflow is modeled on git: a published spec is main, drafts are branches, and proposals are pull requests. It should feel familiar to developers, while making it easy for the whole team to work with specs and keep them up to date without touching git.

It’s still early and there’s plenty to improve, but I’d love to hear your feedback.

records.title: Show HN: AI agent needs process to build a commercial application
records.author: abalgir
records.storyText:
I decided to test this claim with my app, NoMoreHappyPath (NMHP), against Claude on a real project.

Here is the test:

I built Acremuse, a commercial real estate analysis platform, with Claude Desktop and Codex as a reviewer. It is deployed and used today by a couple of investors. Then I wondered what I'd missed that might bite me later.

~ 374,000 Lines of program code - 1,070 Source files (Python and TypeScript) - ~ 11,400 Functions and methods - 3,067 Automated tests

So I gave the same 374k-line code snapshot and the same brief to one Claude session that can use Codex as a reviewer and to my own tool, NMHP. My directive was the same for both: Analyze the code, find any errors/bugs, and list them by severity. Findings must be reviewed before writing the final report.

The Results (Verified by an impartial, blind Codex judge):

NMHP: 33 real issues found. 7 false claims.

Claude: 10 real issues found. 2 false claims.

Only 6 issues overlapped.

Time & Cost: From the owner's go-ahead to the reviewer's pass, NoMoreHappyPath took about 74 minutes, including time lost while it found and worked around a defect in the product itself. The Python version NMHP was working on was 3.9, the OS version, and it didn't have pytest installed, which was needed to verify some claims. After 15 minutes of blockage, the CTO stepped in and told the agent to create a venv with Python 3.13, install the corresponding pytest, and move the project along. NMHP CTO reacts when 15 minutes pass without movement from agents.

To be fair to Claude, Claude did create a venv from the get-go.

Time & Cost: NMHP took 74 minutes and cost $24 in API spend. Claude finished in a few minutes for a fraction of that cost. And yes, NMHP takes over an hour and costs twenty-four bucks. But for a 374k-line codebase, finding 23 more real issues overall that vanilla Claude missed makes $24 a massive win compared to human audit rates.

I know this isn't a benchmark; it's one app and one run each. I wrote a detailed white paper on it.

But it confirmed my idea: an AI agent without a real process is not yet capable of building a commercially ready application, even with a frontier model and reviews that are initiated by the same agent.

records.title: Show HN: Sigflint - AWS SigV4 signing - Node/Bun/Deno/Cloudflare/Browser, 0 deps
records.author: bompus
records.storyText:
I wrote sigflint because I wanted to sign AWS requests from Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers and browsers without pulling in an SDK or any dependencies. It is a single package with no dependencies that signs requests as an Authorization header or a presigned URL, for S3 and any other AWS service. It also does SigV4a (multi-region), chunked uploads and event streams.

What I checked, and how:

* Signatures match botocore for all 3,360 S3 requests in the test corpus, plus 1,622 requests to other services and 1,600 presigned URLs. SigV4a signatures verify against the AWS CRT's, and chunk and event signatures match the AWS SDKs.

* Speed: 1.0 to 3.2 µs per header or presigned-URL signature on Node 26.12.1 and 0.7 to 3.0 µs on Bun 1.4.4; an S3 GET signs in 0.97 µs on Node. The six other libraries I compared took 2x to 75x as long on the requests they sign correctly.

* Size: the bundled, minified header signer is 5.7 kB, 2.8 kB gzipped, and the other signers add to a bundle only when imported.

Feedback on the API or on requests it signs wrongly is welcome: https://github.com/bompus/sigflint/issues

records.title: Show HN: Cb2026, a Rust chess engine that revisits a 2004 world-record project
records.author: cjus
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Carlos. In 2004 Colin Frayn and I ran ChessBrain, a distributed chess computer that played a game against GM Peter Heine Nielsen using machines volunteered from around the world. It set the Guinness World Record for the largest networked chess computer. Some ideas from that project stayed with me, so I created cb2026 (ChessBrain 2026) to explore them.

cb2026 is a chess engine written from scratch in Rust. It speaks UCI and XBoard, so it runs in En Croissant, Cute Chess, XBoard and similar GUIs. It has Lazy SMP search, Syzygy tablebase probing, Polyglot opening books, Chess960, and an NNUE evaluation network trained on its own games.

Strength: about 3379 ± 21 on the CCRL Blitz scale, from 5,600 games against seven rated engines. Its original hand-crafted evaluation rated 2782, and each NNUE generation improved on that.

I wanted it to be easy to learn from as well as strong:

- Every technique can be switched off. An interactive shell lets you play it, watch it think depth by depth, and toggle things like null-move pruning to see what each one does. - docs/elo-ledger.md records how much Elo each technique gained. - A companion book, "Building a Chess Engine in Rust", has a chapter for each stage, from board representation and move generation to NNUE. Each chapter covers the idea, the real code and what it measured. It's free online, as a PDF or as an EPUB: https://cjus.github.io/chessengine/

It also has strength levels that blunder about as often as Lichess players of a given rating do.

License is MIT or Apache-2.0. The one exception: release binaries include Syzygy probing through a GPL-3.0 crate, which makes those binaries GPL. Build with --no-default-features to get a binary with no GPL code.

Happy to answer questions about the engine, the book, or ChessBrain.

records.title: Show HN: Dbprint – Database Context for Agents
records.author: jakubro
records.storyText:
CLI that produces an offline snapshot of a database (DDL, column- and relation-level statistics, values with frequencies), combines it with annotations written by you or an agent, and exposes it as MCP and as a web UI. Works with PG, MySQL, Snowflake, ClickHouse, Databricks, BigQuery.

How to try it:

  uvx dbprint context \
    arboretum.seedbank.germination_trial \
    --purpose query \
    --project https://github.com/jakubro/dbprint/blob/main/docs/format/v1/examples/production/.dbprint.yaml
Features:

- Philosophy: snapshots are meant to sit next to your code and versioned so that you have a history of changes and agents can hit them when searching codebase.

- Offline: no need to expose live credentials to agents.

- CI: "dbprint check" can verify schema/data drift.

- Annotations: complement statistics by documenting the meaning behind data. An agent can prepare them for you ("dbprint annotate").

- Redaction: values can be masked/excluded/hashed either explicitly with FQNs or automatically based on inferred sensitivity and value shape.

- Format: Snapshots are YAML and markdown, so greppable and usable by other tools.

Why I built this: SQL queries produced by agents were inaccurate, and the overall time to result was slow and costly because of finding the answers in codebase or in live database.

records.title: Show HN: Cc-pair – Claude Code and Codex review each other's work
records.author: blackicebird
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built cc-pair because I kept noticing that when a coding agent reviews its own work, it tends to go easy on it. cc-pair pairs the two agents I already use — Claude Code and Codex — so one authors a change and the other reviews it, and they iterate until the reviewer approves or the round limit (default 3) escalates to the human.

Roles are symmetric: either agent can be author or reviewer. In auto mode, `pair start --as claude` (or `--as codex`) opens the author and starts the other agent as reviewer for each round — no second terminal needed. In manual mode you run both yourself. They communicate through numbered message files in a shared directory (~/.pair/<repo>-<hash>/), so the whole review thread is inspectable on disk.

Install: npm install -g claude-codex-pair (Node 22+, macOS/Linux for auto mode; manual mode works on Windows). Both CLIs need to be installed and signed in.

Repo: https://github.com/leonlee/cc-pair — the README has an example review thread in Appendix A, and DESIGN.md specifies the protocol.

I'd love feedback: does cross-model review actually catch things self-review misses in your experience, and what would you want the reviewer to be stricter about?

records.title: Show HN: Convert Anthropic and OpenAI bill exports to FinOps FOCUS (open source)
records.author: manvshinde
records.storyText:
I needed to put our Anthropic and OpenAI spend next to our cloud bills, and found that the exports don't fit together.

The Claude Console gives you two CSVs. The Cost export has dollars rounded to the cent, so a day of cache reads shows $0.00. The Usage export has token counts and no dollars. Anthropic also counts input in four parts that don't overlap: uncached, cache reads, 5-minute cache writes and 1-hour cache writes, priced at 1×, 0.1×, 1.25× and 2× input. OpenAI does it differently: input_tokens already includes cached tokens. If you merge the two exports without accounting for that, you double-count or drop cached input.

FOCUS is the FinOps Foundation's open billing schema. AWS, GCP and Azure already export it, but the official converters don't cover any AI provider yet. So this is a small MIT CLI:

npx ai-bill-to-focus convert cost.csv usage.csv -o focus.csv --check

It writes one row per day, model and token type, each with its own SKU, unit price and quantity. The dollar column is always the provider's own figure. For Anthropic, a row gets the exact token-priced amount only if that rounds to the Cost export's cents; otherwise it keep and a column says which. check runs theFinOps Foundation's validator rules, which I ported to JS, and exits non-zero on errors, so it can gate CI. Rulecan't evaluate are counted and reported, n

Status: Anthropic is tested on real Consolhe cent. OpenAI and Together AI are built from their documented export formats and haven't been run on a real file yet. If you have one and it breaks, theheader row alone is enough for me to fix i

Network: convert downloads a public model the request contains nothing from your files. --offline skips it, and --prices lets you supply your own list. There's also an in-browser version that doesn't upload anything: https://www.cognocient.co

I work on Cognocient AI, which does this kequest (by feature, team or agent run)through a proxy. The CLI works on its own with no account. I'd especially like feedback from anyone already loading FOCUS data into a warehouse.

records.title: Show HN: Ocel – Deploy apps to your AWS,GCP or VPS with infra from code
records.author: vndaba
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I’m Victor and I’ve been building Ocel, an open source CLI, Console and SDK for deploying your apps and the infra they need to your own AWS/GCP/VPS.

The CLI: Run ‘ocel deploy’ in your existing apps, and deploy to a configured target, no separate IaC files required.

The SDK: Declare infra your app needs as code within the app itself, the CLI builds and provisions with no extra steps when deploying. Rust, Go, Python and Typescript supported.

The Console: Optional self-hostable UI for an otherwise CLI-first product. The neat part is that the console itself is an app built with the sdk and deployed with the CLI !

You can try it out to deploy your apps to your own infra. VPS is well tested, and AWS+Cloudflare is also quite well covered. I’ve been dogfooding this myself for things I’m building. Please expect bugs, as it’s still early days.

Why ?

I’ve been a big fan and user of SST for a long time (personal and professional projects). The DX is genuinely unmatched and the high-level components make things quite easy. I think they proved that most apps don’t need complex IaC code, and abstracting things behind high level components/primitives, with some customization levers, actually works quite well.

Ocel builds on that by taking it a bit further, no infra code, have a similar ‘high level components’ approach, but directly in the app. And support deploying existing apps or frameworks from day one in the CLI. You should be able to cd into an existing app and just deploy! (Of course theres a bit more like providing credentials to the platform you are deploying to, domains, one-time setup, etc). Everything else is the gripes I had after deploying tons of apps with SST:

- Preview and production separation built in, so previews can share heavy resources and be considerably faster - First class support for separating the origin and edge, so composing AWS and cloudflare (common setup I had) becomes a breeze - CLI-first product, but with a UI console that can also be self hosted for things like team management, setting env vars, etc. - More SDK primitives (Realtime, Tasks, Pubsub topics, etc) that give a BaaS-like experience no matter where you deploy

records.title: Show HN: MadTracker – Scoring software for track cycling races
records.author: c0nsumer
records.storyText:
Sharing a project I've been working on for the last while, MadTracker, a scoring system for track cycling races:

Announcement: https://nuxx.net/blog/2026/10/29/madtracker/

GitHub w/ Binary Releases: https://github.com/c0nsumer/madtracker

This was built to replace an Excel-based manual scoring system that worked, but was clunky and required specialized knowledge making it hard to hand off to other volunteers at the local velodrome.

MadTracker was developed by formalizing scoring rules from the USA Cycling and other club formats to build a scoring engine, then wrapping it in a front end that holds venue info, event info, rider info, race info, and then makes noting who finished in what order easy. The order and such is run through the scoring engine and this produces results that display on a scoreboard (second monitor), export as PDFs, and export as a CVS for upload to a governing body's scoring website.

I'm really happy with how this came out. It's super niche, but it fills a local need and makes a slice of a small community better, so I wanted to share it.

It's free software, MIT licensed, for macOS / Windows / Linux, doesn't require network connectivity, and aimed at being simple to use while solving the scoring problem.

More info:

Mad Track Arena, Detroit, Michigan, US (our local velodrome): https://madtrackarena.com/

Track Cycling: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_cycling

Race, where an earlier version of MadTracker was in development testing (and can be seen on the scoreboards in the center of the spectator area): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V562MpKpi_o

records.title: Show HN: Sheetgraph, AI agents can understand complex spreadsheets
records.author: asharma327
records.storyText:
Hi guys,

I built a tool www.lovespreadsheets.com earlier this year and a huge problem we kept running into is processing messy, real-world, complex spreadsheets for AI agents.

Even a "medium" sized spreadsheet converts to about 1m+ tokens if read fully, which immediately blows up the current context windows of most models. So I noticed most agents sample data from spreadsheets in chunks instead.

So I (& Claude) built this library Sheetgraph, https://github.com/asharma327/sheetgraph, to compress spreadsheets (~100x compression) while still maintaining their structure (like a dependency graph for formulas) & other relevant metadata such as macros, cell data types, formatting. There is a zipped full workbook of the spreadsheet as well for the agent to lookup data as needed.

Still rough around the edges so would love any feedback on both the idea and any details. This is used in our primary product + services platform Love Spreadsheets so we are actively maintaining and improving it.

Thanks!
